slides.title: Chapter 14: Second-Layer Apps
slides.sub: What the chain guarantees, how a payment channel is built, and how Lightning routes payments

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 and lnd 0.21.3-beta results are one recorded run, read back here.

slides.notes: This deck explains what is built on top of Bitcoin: the guarantees of the chain, colored coins, payment channels and the Lightning Network. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run on private test chains.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Four parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has four parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and nineteen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Four parts, nineteen examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Which guarantees of the chain can an application rely on, and how do two applications mix them?
How can a coin carry a second meaning, and who checks it?
What does a payment channel put on the chain, and what stays off it?
How does a revocation key stop a party from cheating with an old state?
How does an HTLC let a secret open a payment and time return it?
How does Lightning route a payment through strangers and keep the route private?
What does a channel cost, and what does a relay earn?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, four parts
slides.sub: The concept map the whole deck hangs on
slides.notes: The chapter has four parts. Together they hold 61 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.take: Four parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: What the chain guarantees
slides.sub: The chain is a toolbox of guarantees; an application is a recipe.

items.meaning: Guarantees such as no double spend and immutability can be reused by any application.
items.analogy: Think of bricks that fit many buildings.

items.meaning: A digital notary and a crowdfund each mix several guarantees.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe that mixes basic ingredients.

slides.notes: Bitcoin offers guarantees that any application can reuse: no double spend, immutability, timestamps and more. This part lists them, then shows how a digital notary and a crowdfund mix them. We test four of them on a private chain.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (1 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Second-Layer Applications
items.meaning: Services built on Bitcoin's first layer that use its guarantees and change none of its rules.
items.analogy: Think of shops on a busy high street that never rebuild the road.

items.label: Building Blocks (Primitives)
items.meaning: The guarantees Bitcoin offers, which every application may reuse.
items.analogy: Think of bricks that fit many different buildings.

items.label: Applications from Building Blocks
items.meaning: Each application mixes several guarantees, as a digital notary mixes immutability, a timestamp and durability.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe that mixes a few basic ingredients.

items.label: second layer
items.meaning: A system that settles on the chain but does most of its work away from it.
items.analogy: Think of a tram line that meets the main railway at a few stations.

items.label: primitives
items.meaning: The basic guarantees themselves, small enough to be combined in many ways.
items.analogy: Think of the notes of a scale that every song is built from.

items.label: no double spend
items.meaning: No output can be spent twice in the same valid chain of blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that the bank cashes only once.

slides.notes: These cards cover Second-Layer Applications, Building Blocks (Primitives), Applications from Building Blocks, second layer, primitives and no double spend. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A double spend and the fee
slides.sub: Two spends of one coin on a private chain

rows: fees = [d['fee_%s_sat' % k] for k in ks]
groups.note: Bitcoin Core, on a private chain, accepted a first spend of one coin.
A second spend of the same coin with a lower fee was refused, with a named reason.
A second spend with a higher fee replaced the first, and the first vanished.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: fee of each spend, in satoshis
The lower fee is refused: insufficient fee. The higher fee wins, and the first spend is gone: yes.

slides.notes: No output can be spent twice in the same chain. Core accepted a first spend and refused a second one that paid less. It replaced the first with a second that paid more, and the first then vanished from the waiting pool. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Only a spend that pays more can replace the first one

slides.title: Two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins
slides.sub: The first purchase settled on the chain; small ones now travel off it

items.cap: Papa Johns Jacksonville - Sanjev Rajaram, CC0 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 22 May 2010 Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, the first notable retail purchase of physical goods with bitcoin.
WHY: He had offered the coins for a couple of pizzas in a Bitcoin Forum post, and a 19-year-old, Jeremy Sturdivant, took the offer.
HOW: Sturdivant ordered two Papa John's pizzas to Hanyecz's home in Jacksonville and received the coins; the payment settled on the chain.
SO WHAT: A payment on the chain waits for confirmations, which payment channels and Lightning avoid for small payments.

items.body: Picture: the plaque in a Papa John's shop

items.who: Laszlo Hanyecz, a programmer who posted the offer and had contributed to Bitcoin's source code, and Jeremy Sturdivant
items.where: Jacksonville, Florida, USA, where the pizzas were delivered, and the Bitcoin Forum, where the offer was posted

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2010-05-22. On 18 May 2010, by the forum's clock, Laszlo Hanyecz opened the thread Pizza for bitcoins? and offered 10,000 bitcoins for a couple of pizzas delivered to Jacksonville, Florida. The lesson is that the first purchase settled on the chain; small ones now travel off it.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (2 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: immutability
items.meaning: The more work lies on top of a transaction, the more energy it takes to rewrite it.
items.analogy: Think of wet concrete that sets harder every hour.

items.label: neutrality
items.meaning: The network relays any valid transaction with a sufficient fee, whoever sends it.
items.analogy: Think of a post office that stamps every parcel with enough postage.

items.label: secure timestamping
items.meaning: The consensus rules keep block times roughly honest, so a recorded fact has a trusted date.
items.analogy: Think of a postmark that the sender cannot choose.

items.label: authorization
items.meaning: A script that asks for a signature cannot run without the holder of the private key.
items.analogy: Think of a door that opens only to its owner's key.

items.label: auditability
items.meaning: Every transaction is public and links back to the genesis block.
items.analogy: Think of a ledger that anyone may read from the first page.

items.label: accounting
items.meaning: Outputs never exceed inputs, so a transaction cannot create or destroy value.
items.analogy: Think of a till that must balance to the last coin.

slides.notes: These cards cover immutability, neutrality, secure timestamping, authorization, auditability and accounting. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Nonexpiration and accounting
slides.sub: A transaction signed long ago, and one that pays too much

groups.note: A transaction signed 150 blocks earlier was still accepted, because its input was unspent.
A transaction whose outputs exceed its inputs is refused, whatever its signatures say.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: two guarantees put to the test
The old transaction is still valid. The one that pays out more than it takes in is refused with the name bad-txns-in-belowout.

slides.notes: A transaction signed 150 blocks earlier was still valid, because its input was unspent. A transaction whose outputs exceed its inputs was refused, whatever the signatures said. These are two of the chain's guarantees. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A transaction does not expire, and it can never pay out more than it takes in

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (3 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: nonexpiration
items.meaning: A valid transaction stays valid for as long as its inputs are unspent.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque with no expiry date.

items.label: integrity
items.meaning: A signature covers the parts of a transaction it commits to, so they cannot be altered.
items.analogy: Think of a wax seal that breaks if the letter is changed.

items.label: transaction atomicity
items.meaning: A transaction is mined in full or not at all, never halfway.
items.analogy: Think of a light switch: on or off, never half.

items.label: quorum of control
items.meaning: A multisignature script demands a set number of keys, such as two of two.
items.analogy: Think of a safe that needs two keyholders.

items.label: timelock
items.meaning: A script clause can run only after a set time or block height.
items.analogy: Think of a bank vault on a time lock.

items.label: replication
items.meaning: Every full node keeps a copy of the chain, so the data survives local failures.
items.analogy: Think of the same book on the shelves of many libraries.

slides.notes: These cards cover nonexpiration, integrity, transaction atomicity, quorum of control, timelock and replication. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Proof of existence
slides.sub: A document's hash in an OP_RETURN output

groups.note: A transaction can carry the hash of a document in an output that nobody can spend.
The script is OP_RETURN followed by the hash, and the output holds no value.
The block that holds the transaction gives the document a date.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the notary output
The hash is in the chain at block 452, dated 2026-10-15. The document itself is not in the chain.

slides.notes: A transaction can carry the hash of a document in an output that nobody can spend. The script is OP_RETURN and the hash, and the output holds no value. The block that holds the transaction gives the document its date. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A hash in a transaction proves that the document existed at that block's date

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (4 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: forgery protection
items.meaning: A transaction can spend only existing, validated outputs, so value cannot be counterfeited.
items.analogy: Think of a bank that checks every note against its register.

items.label: consistency
items.meaning: The deeper a block lies, the less likely it is to be reorganised.
items.analogy: Think of footprints in drying cement: the older, the firmer.

items.label: recording external state
items.meaning: A transaction can commit to outside data through OP_RETURN or pay to contract.
items.analogy: Think of a notary who stamps a page of someone else's contract.

items.label: predictable issuance
items.meaning: Fewer than 21 million bitcoin will ever exist, issued at a known rate.
items.analogy: Think of a mint that follows a published timetable.

items.label: proof of existence
items.meaning: A document's hash in a transaction proves the document existed when that block was mined.
items.analogy: Think of a notary's date stamp on a sealed envelope.

items.label: Lighthouse
items.meaning: A crowdfunding application whose pledges are signed inputs, spendable only when the goal is met.
items.analogy: Think of a street collection that pays out only when the target is reached.

slides.notes: These cards cover forgery protection, consistency, recording external state, predictable issuance, proof of existence and Lighthouse. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Lighthouse: a crowdfund
slides.sub: Pledges that move only when the goal is met

groups.note: Two pledges, less the fee, make the goal of the fundraiser.
One pledge alone is refused; both pledges together are accepted.
Changing the output breaks the signatures, and a signature of everything stops a late pledge.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: four tries at the fundraiser
The fundraiser can be spent only with all pledges in and the output unchanged.

slides.notes: Two pledges, less the fee, make the goal. One pledge alone is refused, because it pays out more than it takes in. Changing the output breaks the signatures, and a signature over everything stops a pledge that comes too late. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Signatures fix the output, so the money moves only when the goal is reached

slides.title: Colored coins and seals
slides.sub: A colored coin is a banknote stamped with a second meaning.

items.meaning: An unspent output can be tied to a statement only once, when it is spent.
items.analogy: Think of a tamper seal that breaks when opened.

items.meaning: A key is tweaked so that it commits to a contract nobody else sees.
items.analogy: Think of an invisible engraving on a key.

items.meaning: The receiver checks the whole history of an asset; the chain holds only commitments.
items.analogy: Think of a buyer reading a car's service book.

slides.notes: A coin can be marked so that it stands for another asset. Three ideas make that work: a seal that opens once, a key that commits to a contract, and a receiver who checks the history himself. We run two of them.

slides.title: Colored coins and seals: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Colored Coins
items.meaning: A small amount of bitcoin is marked so that it stands for another asset, such as a share.
items.analogy: Think of a banknote stamped 'this is a stock certificate'.

items.label: Single-Use Seals
items.meaning: A data structure that can be tied to another only once; an unspent output does that.
items.analogy: Think of a tamper seal on a parcel that breaks when opened.

items.label: Pay to Contract (P2C)
items.meaning: A public key is tweaked so that it commits to a contract that nobody else sees.
items.analogy: Think of a key with an invisible engraving of the agreement.

items.label: Client-Side Validation
items.meaning: The receiver checks the whole history of an asset; the chain holds only commitments.
items.analogy: Think of a buyer who reads a car's whole service book.

items.label: RGB
items.meaning: A colored coin protocol made to work with channels, built from seals, contracts and client checks.
items.analogy: Think of a club with its own rules, meeting in a public hall.

items.label: Taproot Assets
items.meaning: A colored coin protocol, once called Taro, built around taproot-style contracts.
items.analogy: Think of foreign banknotes carried on the same railway.

slides.notes: These cards cover Colored Coins, Single-Use Seals, Pay to Contract (P2C), Client-Side Validation, RGB and Taproot Assets. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Client-side validation
slides.sub: A token history that the chain never shows

rows: outs = len({h['outpoint'] for h in c['history']})
groups.note: The history of ACME tokens names two transactions and three outputs.
Each step commits to its contract; a forged contract does not match.
Yet nothing in the chain shows that any token exists.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the history of the ACME tokens
The chain shows ordinary outputs only. The receiver must read the history to know what they mean.

slides.notes: The history of ACME tokens passes through two transactions. Each one commits to its contract, and a forged contract does not match. Yet nothing in the chain shows that the tokens exist, so the receiver must check the whole history. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The chain holds a commitment, and the receiver checks the history

slides.title: Colored coins and seals: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: native forwarding
items.meaning: Every hop on a Lightning path must know the asset and hold a balance of it.
items.analogy: Think of a relay in which every courier handles the special parcel.

items.label: translated forwarding
items.meaning: Only the first and last hops know the asset, and the hops between forward plain bitcoin.
items.analogy: Think of exchange booths at both ends of a bridge, plain coins in the middle.

slides.notes: These cards cover native forwarding and translated forwarding. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Pay to contract
slides.sub: A tweaked key that commits to a contract

groups.note: A key tweaked by a contract gives another address than the plain key.
Revealing the contract and the tweak proves the commitment; a wrong contract fails.
Only the tweaked key can spend the output; the plain key cannot.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: a key tweaked by a contract
The reveal proves the commitment only for the real contract, and only the tweaked key spends.

slides.notes: A public key is tweaked by a contract and looks like any other key. Revealing the key and the contract proves the commitment; a wrong contract fails. The output can be spent only with the tweaked key, never with the plain one. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Only the holder of the contract can reveal the commitment and spend

slides.title: Payment channels
slides.sub: A payment channel is a bar tab: many small orders, one bill at closing time.

items.meaning: Two transactions on the chain, and any number of signed updates between them.
items.analogy: Think of opening and closing a bar tab.

items.meaning: Each side's payout is delayed, and an old state can be punished with a revocation key.
items.analogy: Think of a contract that forfeits the safe to a cheat.

items.meaning: A secret claims the payment before a deadline; after it the payer takes the money back.
items.analogy: Think of a locker with a code and a return date.

slides.notes: Two people can trade many times and settle once. This part builds a channel step by step: a funding output, refunds, commitments that punish an old state, and a secret that claims a payment. Each step is run on a private chain.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (1 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Payment Channels and State Channels
items.meaning: Two parties exchange signed transactions off the chain and settle on it later.
items.analogy: Think of a bar tab that is paid once, at closing time.

items.label: State Channels - Basic Concepts and Terminology
items.meaning: A funding transaction opens the channel, commitments change it, and a settlement closes it.
items.analogy: Think of opening, using and paying a hotel bill.

items.label: Simple Payment Channel Example
items.meaning: Emma pays Fabian for each second of video, and a signed refund protects her.
items.analogy: Think of a taxi meter that counts up while you ride.

items.label: Making Trustless Channels
items.meaning: Signed refunds and lock times let each side leave safely without trusting the other.
items.analogy: Think of a deposit with a clause that returns it by a set date.

items.label: Asymmetric Revocable Commitments
items.meaning: Each side holds a commitment that delays its own payout and can be punished once it is old.
items.analogy: Think of a contract that hands the safe to the other party if you cheat.

items.label: Hash Time Lock Contracts (HTLC)
items.meaning: A secret can claim the payment before a deadline, and the payer can reclaim it after.
items.analogy: Think of a locker opened by a code today, reclaimed by its owner tomorrow.

slides.notes: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Payment channels. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Emma and Fabian's channel
slides.sub: A two-of-two output funded by Emma

groups.note: Emma funds one hour of video at 1,000 satoshis a second: 3,600,000 satoshis.
Spending the funding output needs both signatures; Emma alone is refused.
The script starts with 2 and ends with 2 and CHECKMULTISIG: two of two.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the funding output of the channel
Opcode 52 is OP_2 and ae is CHECKMULTISIG: two keys must sign, so Emma cannot run off with the funds.

slides.notes: Emma funds one hour of video, at 1,000 satoshis a second. The funding output is a two-of-two script. Emma alone cannot spend it, and both together can. The witness script begins with a 2 and ends with a 2 and CHECKMULTISIG. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The funding output needs both keys, so neither side can spend alone

slides.title: The first payment channels
slides.sub: Channels began as a replaced transaction waiting for its lock time

items.cap: Micropayment channel - Burchert, Decker, Wattenhofer, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Mike Hearn posted Anti DoS for tx replacement on 17 April 2013, and Jeremy Spillman answered on 20 April with a one-way channel design.
WHY: The first Bitcoin code already let an unrecorded open transaction be replaced until its lock time, and the channel idea grew from that.
HOW: The payer signs larger and larger payments while a refund waits behind a lock time; Hearn and Matt Corallo announced bitcoinj code on 27 June 2013.
SO WHAT: Such channels were safe only with segwit transactions, so Emma's refund is signed before the funding is sent.

items.body: Picture: a later authors' channel diagram

items.who: Mike Hearn, who posted Anti DoS for tx replacement on 17 April 2013, Jeremy Spillman, who answered on 20 April 2013, and Matt Corallo
items.where: the bitcoin-development mailing list, BitcoinTalk.org and the bitcoinj library
items.linkText: Reply: Anti DoS for tx replacement (list post)

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2013-04-20. The Bitcoin Wiki traces payment channels to the first Bitcoin code, where an unrecorded open transaction could keep being replaced until its lock time, and to a personal email of Satoshi Nakamoto that described it. The lesson is that channels began as a replaced transaction, waiting for its lock time.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (2 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: payment channel
items.meaning: Two parties keep a running balance of signed transactions that they do not publish.
items.analogy: Think of a running tab between two friends.

items.label: state channel
items.meaning: The general form: any shared state is changed off the chain and secured by a final settlement.
items.analogy: Think of a score sheet that both players sign after every point.

items.label: funding transaction
items.meaning: The one transaction that locks the shared funds in a two-of-two output and opens the channel.
items.analogy: Think of the deposit paid into a joint account.

items.label: commitment transaction
items.meaning: A signed transaction that could be published but is held back and replaced by newer ones.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque kept in a drawer and replaced by a newer one.

items.label: settlement transaction
items.meaning: The final transaction that closes the channel and pays each side its share.
items.analogy: Think of the final bill at checkout.

items.label: refund transaction
items.meaning: A signed, time-locked transaction that returns the funds if the channel never starts.
items.analogy: Think of the return ticket bought before the journey.

slides.notes: These cards cover payment channel, state channel, funding transaction, commitment transaction, settlement transaction and refund transaction. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Refunds with falling lock times
slides.sub: Six signed refunds; the newest becomes valid first

groups.note: Six refunds were signed, each with a lower lock time than the one before.
At the start every one of them is refused as not yet final.
The newest refund is refused six blocks early and accepted five blocks before.

Six blocks early the newest refund is not yet final; five blocks early it is accepted.

Six blocks before the newest lock time it is still refused, and five blocks before it is accepted. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (3 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Spillman-style payment channel
items.meaning: A one-way channel of 2013: ever larger signed payments, and a refund behind a lock time.
items.analogy: Think of a prepaid card that only goes down, with a refund date.

items.label: revocation key
items.meaning: A key of two secret halves that lets the wronged side take the whole channel after a cheat.
items.analogy: Think of a spare key to the cheater's safe, held by the victim.

items.label: asymmetric commitment
items.meaning: The two commitments differ: the holder's own payout waits, the other side is paid at once.
items.analogy: Think of two cheques where only the signer has to wait.

items.label: preimage
items.meaning: The secret that hashes to the value in an HTLC; whoever knows it can claim the payment.
items.analogy: Think of the original text behind a published fingerprint.

slides.notes: These cards cover Spillman-style payment channel, revocation key, asymmetric commitment and preimage. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Balances move, capacity stays
slides.sub: A channel of 100 units after three payments

groups.note: A channel of 100 units starts with everything on Alice's side.

rows: tot = {a + b for a, b in hist}
left = [a for a, b in hist]
groups.note: Each move shifts value between the two sides; their sum never changes.
The left column is Alice's balance after each step, and the sum stays at 100.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: Alice's balance after each payment
Bob holds the rest each time. The two balances always add up to 100.

slides.notes: A channel's capacity is fixed when it is funded. Each payment only shifts value from one side to the other, so the sum of the two balances never changes. A payment larger than the sender's balance cannot be made. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The two balances always add up to the capacity of the channel

slides.title: On the chain, or off it?
slides.sub: Why a channel is cheap and fast, and what it still needs from the chain

left.head: On the chain
rows: The funding transaction opens the channel.
The settlement closes it for good.
Like the deposit and the final bill.

right.head: Off the chain
rows: No one else sees them, and fees are small.
Like the running tab in between.

slides.notes: A channel puts two transactions on the chain, the funding and the settlement. Everything between them stays off the chain as signed commitments. The chain is the court of last resort, which is why each side keeps its latest commitment.
slides.take: Two transactions on the chain, and any number of updates between them

slides.title: A commitment that can be punished
slides.sub: The delayed output of a commitment transaction

The cheater must wait 1000 blocks, while the victim holding both halves can take the output at once.

slides.title: An HTLC: a secret or the clock
slides.sub: Who can claim a hash time lock contract, and when

rows: h = R['c5']; a = lambda k: h[k]['allowed']
groups.note: The right secret and the receiver's key claim the output; the payer's key does not.
The refund works only at the lock height, nineteen blocks after funding.
A wrong secret fails the hash check, whoever signs.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: who can claim the HTLC
The secret opens it for the receiver. The clock opens it for the payer, but only at the lock height.

slides.notes: The receiver claims the output with the secret and a signature. A wrong secret fails the hash check, and the payer's key cannot claim it. The payer's refund is final only at the lock height, nineteen blocks after funding. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: The Lightning Network
slides.sub: Lightning is a chain of couriers who pass a parcel on and each keep a small fee.

items.meaning: A payment crosses several channels, and each relay keeps a small fee.
items.analogy: Think of parcel couriers who each take a fee.

items.meaning: The sender wraps the path in layers, and each relay peels exactly one.
items.analogy: Think of pass-the-parcel at a party.

items.meaning: A payee's invoice names an amount and a hash; the BOLTs are the shared standards.
items.analogy: Think of a bill and the plug standards.

slides.notes: Lightning links channels into a network. We follow a payment through relays, count the fees and the time locks, read an invoice and a packet, and watch a breach being punished. Every number comes from the recorded run or the specification.

slides.title: The Lightning Network: key concepts (1 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Routed Payment Channels (Lightning Network)
items.meaning: Many channels linked end to end, so that anyone can pay anyone through intermediaries.
items.analogy: Think of a chain of couriers who pass a parcel hand to hand.

items.label: Basic Lightning Network Example
items.meaning: Alice pays Eric one bitcoin through Bob, Carol and Diana, who each keep a small fee.
items.analogy: Think of parcel relays where each courier takes a fee.

items.label: Lightning Network Transport and Pathfinding
items.meaning: Nodes talk over encrypted links, share channel news by flooding, and the sender plans the path.
items.analogy: Think of a driver who plans a route from a shared road map.

items.label: Lightning Network Benefits
items.meaning: Privacy, fungibility, speed, granularity, capacity and trustless operation.
items.analogy: Think of express lanes beside an old toll road.

items.label: Lightning Network
items.meaning: A network of payment channels that routes payments with hash time locks and onion packets.
items.analogy: Think of pneumatic tubes in an office building.

items.label: route
items.meaning: The chain of channels from payer to payee that a payment will follow.
items.analogy: Think of the stops of a bus line.

slides.notes: These cards cover Routed Payment Channels (Lightning Network), Basic Lightning Network Example, Lightning Network Transport and Pathfinding, Lightning Network Benefits, Lightning Network and route. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Satoshis passed from hand to hand
slides.sub: Satoshis passed hand to hand without touching the chain

items.cap: Jack Dorsey 2009 - Brian Solis, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 19 January 2019 the Twitter user hodlonaut began a game-like test of Lightning by sending 100,000 satoshis to a trusted recipient.
WHY: It was a promotional test, passed from one well-known person to the next, to show that the network could carry real payments.
HOW: Each recipient added 10,000 satoshis, 34 cents then, and sent the sum on; Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee, Elizabeth Stark and Changpeng Zhao took part.
SO WHAT: Each hand-over was an ordinary Lightning payment, with no transaction on the chain for each step.

items.body: Picture: Jack Dorsey, 2009, a recipient

items.who: hodlonaut, a pseudonymous Twitter user who began the game, and the recipients who passed it on, among them Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee
items.where: Twitter, and the Lightning Network, where each payment was sent

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2019-01-19. On 19 January 2019 the pseudonymous Twitter user hodlonaut began a game-like promotional test of the Lightning Network by sending 100,000 satoshis, 0.001 bitcoin, to a trusted recipient. The lesson is that lightning payments pass hand to hand without touching the chain.

slides.title: The Lightning Network: key concepts (2 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: invoice
items.meaning: A payee's request for payment that carries an amount, a payment hash and an expiry.
items.analogy: Think of a bill with the payer's reference printed on it.

items.label: onion routing
items.meaning: The sender wraps the path in layers, and each relay peels one and sees only the next hop.
items.analogy: Think of pass-the-parcel at a party.

items.label: Sphinx
items.meaning: The packet format of the Lightning onion: fixed in size, with a check value for every hop.
items.analogy: Think of an envelope of one size, so thin and thick letters look alike.

items.label: BOLT
items.meaning: Basis of Lightning Technology: the numbered specifications that let different programs work together.
items.analogy: Think of plug standards that let any appliance fit any socket.

items.label: pathfinding
items.meaning: Choosing a route with enough capacity and low fees, using the channel announcements.
items.analogy: Think of a satnav that knows how wide each road is.

slides.notes: These cards cover invoice, onion routing, Sphinx, BOLT and pathfinding. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 14.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.sub: The expiry of the HTLC on each hop

Neighbours differ by 80 blocks, and the last two share one expiry. The library agrees: yes.

slides.title: A paper that became a network
slides.sub: A design on paper took years, soft forks and four teams

items.cap: Lightning cut nodes - FrankAndProust, CC0 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja published a Lightning Network white paper in February 2015; the draft kept on lightning.network is version 0.5.9.2.
WHY: Their summary calls it a decentralized system for instant, high-volume micropayments that removes the risk of trusting third-party custody.
HOW: Lightning Labs launched the network in 2018; the picture shows its cut nodes, from under 100 in 2018 to about 1,500 in 2022.
SO WHAT: The book says the network was first described in February 2015; the word proposed no longer holds.

items.body: Picture: the network's cut nodes, approximate

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2015-02-28. Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja published a Lightning Network white paper in February 2015, and Wikipedia cites a copy of version 0.5 archived on 28 February 2015. The lesson is that a design on paper took years, soft forks and four teams.

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: fee

items.label: capacity
items.meaning: The sum locked in a channel; a payment must fit in the balance on the sending side.
items.analogy: Think of a pipe that carries no more than its width.

slides.sub: The parts of a BOLT 4 packet

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each provable from its slides

items: The chain guarantees no double spend, immutability and more, and applications are recipes that mix these guarantees.
Colored coins use a seal, a contract-committing key and client-side checks, so the chain never sees the asset.
A payment channel needs two transactions on the chain, and signed commitments in between.
A revocation key punishes an old state, and an HTLC lets a secret claim a payment before a deadline.
Lightning routes a payment through relays that each keep a fee and have less time than the one before.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all nineteen examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
